notes: Chunk C: topics M2.S17-S20 (nets of other solids, shortest paths on a cuboid) and M3.S21-S24 (projections, front/top/side views, Figure it Out Q1-Q3). 17 units, 23 items.

Worked examples C46, C47, C60-C63 are none: numeric or name answers (circumference, fraction, sqrt(5^2-3^2), names of solids); their teaching figure already sits in the same concept. C48, C51, C52, C64, C65 are required: the answer is a net, an unfolding with the path, or drawn views.
C58 question is optional: all numbers are in the words; the box with the ant and the laddu would help (see its reason) but is not added.

C70 (match objects with their views): both sides none, NOT_RENDERABLE: the book table is 8 illustrated objects and 24 silhouettes. Matching read from the page: jug row 8, funnel row 6, hammer row 7, car row 1, slide row 3, chair row 4, ceiling fan row 5, pressure cooker row 2.

C69 solution table (21 views): the LP gives no sizes, so proportions are chosen in the spec; the ridge line of the prism top view and the edge line of the parallelepiped top view are the only extra visible lines.

C67 question text says 'Fig. 4.6' but the diagram is the table of views of the three lines of that figure (book page 23): needs_lp_text_sync is true, the wording could say 'the three lines whose views are shown'.

C57, C68: the solution figure is a different view from the question figure (net / 3D box with projections); derived_from is set because the validator requires it, the labels (ant, laddu, a, b, c) and numbers are the same.
Folding checks (octahedron net C48, tetrahedron shapes C49/C50) were run in code; the net 2 line of C59 was checked to stay inside the net.

figure_inventory.description: Four shapes of equilateral triangles in a row (checked on the page picture and at 2x zoom): (1) a large triangle cut into 4; (2) a band of 3 triangles (up, down, up) with a 4th hanging below the first, all 4 meeting at one vertex; (3) a straight strip of 4; (4) the strip of 4 with a 5th triangle hanging below its first. Folding check run in code: (1) and (3) fold into a tetrahedron, (2) overlaps (2 triangles on one face; 4 triangles meet at one vertex), (4) has 5 triangles (4 of them also meet at one vertex). Drawn as the question figure of C49 (2 by 2 grid instead of one row) and marked in the C50 solution figure.

Cylinder with the cut along its height and the two circles taken off, beside its net: one rectangle (no lengths printed) with a circle above and a circle below. Teaching figure of the concept 'Unrolling a cylinder'; the worked example C46 itself is none.
Cone with apex O and the slit line l (dashed) from O to the base. Teaching figure of the concept 'Unrolling a cone'; the worked example C47 is none.
The unrolled cone: a sector of a circle (about 220 degrees, not printed) with centre O. Teaching figure of 'Unrolling a cone' (the concept image shows the half-circle case).

Shaded octahedron (8 triangular faces, 6 vertices, hidden edges dashed). Used only to introduce the solid; the LP defines the octahedron in words ('two square pyramids joined at their square bases') in C48, so the picture is not needed.

CHECKED at 4x zoom and by folding in code: the book's octahedron net is a band of 6 triangles (up, down, up, down, up, down) with 1 triangle up on the middle top side and 1 triangle down on the middle bottom side. It is also exactly two fans of 4 triangles (top fan around the right-hand vertex of the top edge, bottom fan around the left-hand vertex of the bottom edge) joined along one edge, as the LP steps say. Drawn for the worked example C48 with the fans coloured.
Shaded dodecahedron (pentagonal faces). Only illustrates a remark; the number 43,380 is in the text and no item asks about the picture.

Cuboid with the laddu at the centre of the top face and the ant at the centre of the right face. The LP worked example C51 states both positions in words; the figure it needs is the flattened net (P16-path_net-1, left net).

Cuboid with the laddu at the middle of the top front edge and the ant at the centre of the right face. C52 states the positions in words; the figure it needs is the flattened net (P16-path_net-2). Note: the LP puts the ant on the front face and the laddu on the top-right edge, the same problem with the two faces named the other way round.
Two cuboids with a red and a blue candidate path ('are either of these the shortest path?'). No LP item asks about these two paths; the same paths are on the nets P16-path_net-1 and P16-path_net-2.

Two identical cross-shaped nets. Left net: laddu at the centre of the 2nd face, ant at the centre of the right arm, a straight red line (case 1, the laddu at the centre of the top face). Right net: the blue two-piece path of case 2. Drawn for C51 as the left net, reduced to the two faces that matter for the 4 cm cube (top face above the side face).

The same net with the laddu at the middle of the bottom edge of the 2nd face and the ant in the right arm; a slanted red straight line (the shortest) and a blue path along the edge then up. Drawn for C52 as the right face laid beside the front face with the straight line, for the 6 cm cube.
The two paths of the net figure drawn on the cuboid (laddu at the middle of the edge). Same figure as P16-path_net-2 shown on the solid; the net version is the one drawn for C52.

Cuboid 8 cm x 4 cm x 4 cm (labels '8 cm', '4 cm', '4 cm'), ant at the centre of the right end face, laddu on the bottom front edge with '2 cm' marked from the right end (checked on the page picture). Drawn as the question figure of C56 without the long arrow texts.
The failed unfolding: a straight line from the laddu to the ant that leaves the net. The LP solution of C56 uses only the working unfolding and never mentions this one, so no item uses the picture.

The unfolding that works: column of four 8 by 4 rectangles, left square on the 2nd, right square (ant) on the 3rd, laddu on the line between the 3rd and 4th rectangle 2 cm from the right end, straight red line inside the net. Drawn as the solution figure of C57 with the numbers of the LP steps (2, 4, sqrt(20) = about 4.47).

30 cm x 12 cm x 12 cm box with the laddu on the back end face (centred, 1 cm above the bottom) and the ant on the front end face (centred, 1 cm below the top). The C58 question is optional (all its numbers are in the words); the box would help but is not added. The positions come back in the solution nets (C59).

Two nets of the 30 x 12 x 12 box: left a T-shape with the straight 42 cm line through the top strip; right with the ant's square on the right of row 1 and the laddu's square on the left of row 3, the 40 cm slanted line and its 32 cm and 24 cm legs (the right angle sits outside the net). Drawn to scale from the 3D facts (ant 1 cm from its shared edge, laddu 1 cm from its shared edge, both centred), as the solution figure of C59.
Point P, plane M and its projection O, right angle POX. Teaching figure; the definition is given in words and no item asks about it.

Fig. 4.2: a line parallel to the plane and a tilted line with their projections and dashed projectors. Teaching figure of 'Projecting a point and a line' (the concept image shows the stick over the table with its projection).

Fig. 4.3: line AB of length l, its projection DC of length p, AE perpendicular to BC so AECD is a rectangle. Teaching figure; the concept image redraws the same right triangle with 5 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm.
Fig. 4.4: a cube and its projection on a plane. Teaching figure; no item asks about it.
Fig. 4.5: a cone and its triangular projection on a plane. Teaching figure; C62 uses the cone standing on its base (circle on the floor), which is its own concept image.

Fig. 4.6 upper drawing: three different lines with the same projection on a plane. The question C67 refers to these lines, but what it asks about is their front, top and side views, which are in P23-views_table-1; the 3D drawing adds nothing the question needs.
Fig. 4.6 lower drawing: a cuboid of three cubes (can be read as cuboids 1, 2, 3 cubes long) and their common projection. Teaching figure; no item asks about it.

Wire box with the vertical, horizontal and side planes, a stack of 3 cubes (two at the bottom, one on the right one) and its three views on the planes. Teaching figure of 'Three planes, three views' (the concept image uses a cylinder).

CORRECTED: side-view lengths measured from the page picture are about 1/9 and 0.3 of the box width, not 1/6 and 2/6. Pixel measurement: 3 x 3 boxes of 144 x 101 px. Front column: the same horizontal line, 95 px, in all three. Top column: row 1 horizontal 95 px; row 2 slanting down 17 px over 97 px; row 3 slanting down 36 px over 96 px. Side column: a dot; a horizontal line of 16 px (about 1/9 of the box, not 1/6); a horizontal line of 44 px (about 0.3 of the box). Drawn as the question figure of C67 with the top-view slope set equal to the side-view length so each row is exact.
Front, top and side views of the three cuboids of Fig. 4.6 (square front face, depths 1, 2, 3). Teaching figure; the Figure it Out question C67 is about the lines, not the cuboids.

Eight coloured illustrations (jug, funnel, hammer, car, slide, chair, ceiling fan, pressure cooker) with T/F/S arrows, beside three columns FRONT, TOP, SIDE of 8 black silhouettes each in shuffled order (checked on the page picture): jug row 8, funnel row 6, hammer row 7, car row 1, slide row 3, chair row 4, ceiling fan row 5, pressure cooker row 2. Illustrated line art that cannot be redrawn faithfully, so C70 (question and solution) gets no diagram.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Unrolling a cylinder
items.question_text: A cylinder has radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Find the sides of the rectangle in its net, using pi as 22/7.
items.reason: Numbers only: circumference 2 x 22/7 x 7 = 44 cm and height 10 cm are computed in the steps; the net of a cylinder is already the teaching image of this concept (shown beside the example), so a second picture adds nothing the student needs to solve it.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Unrolling a cone
items.question_text: A cone has base radius 5 cm and slant length 10 cm. What fraction of a full circle of radius 10 cm is its unrolled curved surface?
items.reason: The question asks for a fraction: 10 pi / 20 pi = 1/2 follows from two circumferences written in the steps. The unrolled sector is the teaching image of this concept, so no separate picture is needed.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Practice: nets beyond the cube
items.question_text: An octahedron is two square pyramids joined at their square bases. Plan a net for it with equilateral triangles, and count its faces, edges and vertices.
items.reason: The example asks to plan a net, so the net itself is the answer; the steps only describe it in words (two fans of 4 triangles joined along one edge) and cannot be followed without seeing the 8 triangles. Drawn as the book's own octahedron net (page 14), which is exactly this two-fan net.

items.question_text: A stick 5 cm long is held above a table so that one end is 3 cm higher than the other. How long is its projection on the table?
items.reason: A right triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is described in one sentence and solved with sqrt(5^2 - 3^2) = 4; the picture of the stick, projection and height is the teaching image of this concept.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Projections of a square and a parallelogram

items.reason: The answer is a shape named with its sides (a rectangle 5 cm by 4 cm), found by the same sqrt(5^2 - 3^2) = 4; nothing has to be drawn and the tilted card is the teaching image of this concept.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Same projection, different objects
items.question_text: A cone standing on its base has base radius 4 cm. Name three different solids whose projection on the floor is the same circle.
items.reason: The answer is a list of names (a cylinder, a ball and a bowl, each of radius 4 cm); the cone, cylinder and ball picture is the teaching image of this concept.

items.lp_book_number: Worked example: Practice: predict the projection
items.question_text: A rod 13 cm long is held above a table so that one end is 5 cm higher than the other. Predict the length of its projection, and say when the projection would be 13 cm.
items.reason: Pure arithmetic: sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = sqrt(144) = 12, plus a one-line rule about a rod parallel to the table; the tilted-and-parallel rod picture is the teaching image of this concept.
